summary: Defines the Remote Direct Memory Access Protocol, which runs over DDP and offers read and write services so data goes directly into application buffers without extra copies. It allows kernel bypass. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RDMAP lets an application send data to a remote computer's memory or retrieve data from it. The protocol uses advertised buffers and defines when data is placed, delivered to an application, or treated as an error.

questions: what is an stag in rdma
subtitle: A protocol for placing data in a remote computer's memory with fewer copies.

tldr.problem: Copying data between applications and network buffers can add latency and consume processor and memory resources.
tldr.mechanism: RDMAP runs over DDP and defines Send, Write, Read, and Terminate operations. Tagged buffers let a peer address a previously advertised memory region.
tldr.outcome: RDMAP defines direct placement and delivery behavior, ordering, headers, and error handling. It is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 7146.

today: RFC 5040 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2007. The unit metadata says it is updated by RFC 7146.

sections.title: Purpose and Protocol Layers
sections.content:
The Remote Direct Memory Access Protocol (RDMAP) allows a local application to read or write a remote computer's memory while preserving memory protection. Its goal is to reduce data copies, latency, and CPU work.

RDMAP runs over Direct Data Placement (DDP). DDP runs over a lower-layer protocol, including MPA over TCP or SCTP. RDMAP, DDP, and MPA together are called iWARP.
sections.plainLanguage: RDMAP is the top layer in a protocol stack for moving data directly between application buffers. Lower layers carry the data and place it in the requested memory.

sections.title: Tagged and Untagged Buffers
sections.content:
A tagged buffer is a memory region that its owner advertises to a remote peer using a Steering Tag (STag), offset, and length. The upper-layer protocol decides how to communicate this information. An untagged buffer is not advertised and is used for control messages and Send operations.

DDP distinguishes placement, which writes data into a buffer and may occur out of order, from delivery, which tells an upper-layer protocol that a message is available. RDMAP uses untagged queue 0 for Send, queue 1 for Read Requests, and queue 2 for Terminate.
sections.plainLanguage: A tagged buffer has an identifier and location that the owner has shared with a peer. An untagged buffer is not shared this way and carries messages such as Sends and Read Requests.

sections.title: The RDMAP Operations
sections.content:
RDMAP defines seven operations: Send, Send with Invalidate, Send with Solicited Event, Send with Solicited Event and Invalidate, RDMA Write, RDMA Read, and Terminate. The four Send forms place data in an untagged buffer; the Invalidate forms also revoke access to an STag, and Solicited Event forms may trigger a receiver event.

RDMA Write places data in a previously advertised tagged buffer. RDMA Read uses one untagged request and one tagged response to copy data from a remote tagged buffer into a local one. Terminate reports an error and ends the stream.
sections.plainLanguage: Send delivers data to an unadvertised buffer; Write places data in an advertised buffer; Read retrieves data from one. Terminate reports an error and stops further communication on the stream.

sections.title: Control Fields and Read Requests
sections.content:
RDMAP uses the first octet reserved for upper-layer use in the DDP header as its control field. The field identifies the RDMAP version and operation code. Send operations that invalidate a buffer also carry the STag to invalidate.

Only the RDMA Read Request and Terminate messages add an RDMAP header. A Read Request identifies the source and destination tagged buffers, their offsets, and the requested size. The size field is 32 bits, and one request can read from zero through 2^32 - 1 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Most RDMAP messages use DDP's header space rather than an extra RDMAP header. A Read Request includes the buffer identifiers, offsets, and amount of data to retrieve.

sections.title: Ordering, Completion and Errors
sections.content:
Messages on different RDMAP streams have no defined ordering, and placement into buffers may happen out of order. An application must wait for delivery of a Send or Read Response before it assumes the relevant data is ready. A later Write may affect the data returned by an outstanding Read; an upper-layer protocol can fence that Write until Read Responses are delivered.

RDMAP does not recover from RDMAP or DDP errors. It reports an error with Terminate and tears down the stream; outstanding message state may be indeterminate. A sender must send no further messages on that stream after sending Terminate.
sections.plainLanguage: Data can be placed before an application is told that it is ready, so applications must wait for delivery. When a protocol error occurs, RDMAP reports it and closes the stream instead of trying to continue.

sections.title: Memory Protection and Network Security
sections.content:
An RNIC must restrict each stream to authorized memory. It must prevent access outside the buffer enabled for a Steering Tag and choose STag values that are difficult to predict. A privileged resource manager controls allocation of scarce resources.

Network packets can be spoofed, changed, or disclosed. The RFC requires compliant implementations to meet the applicable IPsec requirements, including ESP with replay protection. It notes that TLS above RDMAP would not protect the RDMAP headers.
sections.plainLanguage: Remote memory access must be limited to buffers that an application has authorized. IPsec can protect packets against spoofing, changes, and disclosure while they travel across the network.
